transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Julia Chen (Redwood SE), Ethan Kim (CTO, ApolloTech), Priya Rao (SRE Lead), Mark Lyle (Head of Platform)
---
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Ethan Kim: Ethan here.
[00:09] Priya Rao: Priya here.
[00:11] Mark Lyle: Mark, hi.
[00:13] Julia Chen: Julia here from the infra side. Hi all.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Great. The goal today is to understand your reliability requirements, how you'd like failover to behave, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes sense. We'll keep it high-level then follow up with a tech deep dive.
[00:30] Ethan Kim: Sounds good. Quick context: we're rolling chat + recommendations into our e-commerce flow. Peak traffic during sales can be ~4k req/s, baseline ~400 req/s, token rates high because people ask big context. Our SRE org wants p95 response under 500ms and 99.9% availability for the inference endpoint.
[00:50] Priya Rao: And importantly we need deterministic behavior during region outages — can't have total outage for checkout flows.
[00:58] Julia Chen: What counts as an outage for you? Full region down, network blips, or a model serving saturating?
[01:06] Priya Rao: All of the above, but the biggest fear is a cloud region outage. We want multi-region routing and an explicit runbook for failover.
[01:14] Samir Patel: Totally. Redwood supports multi-region routing and policy-based fallbacks. We can route by latency, cost, or tier. In practice for Dedicated customers we recommend active-active in two regions with a primary and warm secondary. On region failure, traffic flips with health-check-driven routing and circuit breakers.
[01:33] Mark Lyle: Active-active — do you replicate KV caches across regions? Our recommender relies on KV cache to keep latency low.
[01:40] Julia Chen: Great question. Our KV cache is per-region for performance; we do async replication for cold starts and warm pools. For strict consistency use-cases we recommend pinning session-affinity to a region or using a thin sync layer.
[01:52] Priya Rao: Async replication means some cold starts after failover, which might spike latency. How do you mitigate that?
[01:58] Julia Chen: We have a few levers — warm pools (pre-warmed replicas), on-failover pre-fetch of common prefixes, and cached fallback responses for high-frequency queries. Also batching and adaptive concurrency controls to avoid thundering herds.
[02:14] Ethan Kim: What's the expected failover time? We need an RTO target for business continuity planning.
[02:20] Samir Patel: For active-active with health checks and automated routing, typical traffic failover is in the 30s to low minutes range depending on DNS TTLs and client retry behavior. With our Dedicated reserved capacity and regional standby, you can hit sub-60s for most traffic. If you want sub-30s you can adopt our edge routing layer + explicit client retry with our SDK which will try secondary endpoints immediately.
[02:42] Priya Rao: And how about SLA? We want a written SLA — 99.9% isn't helpful without definitions (regional vs global).
[02:49] Samir Patel: Absolutely. Our Dedicated plans offer SLA options: 99.9% per-region availability for the endpoint, and we can discuss global availability targets for active-active setups. For Hosted the standard is 99.5% with an availability SLO. We'll share the exact legal language in the security pack.
[03:06] Mark Lyle: When you say fallback policies, what are the typical strategies? We need to understand tradeoffs: lower cost/latency vs hallucination risk.
[03:14] Julia Chen: Common fallbacks: 1) model variant fallback — route to a smaller but compatible model (e.g., 7B optimized) when the preferred model is saturated; 2) cached answers for known prompts; 3) degrade to a lightweight heuristic or rule-based response for critical flows (like checkout confirmation); 4) shed load by returning a 503 or quick error with grace messaging. Each has tradeoffs. Model fallback reduces quality but keeps service live.
[03:38] Ethan Kim: Can we define per-route policies? For checkout we want zero model degradation — maybe block requests or fallback to cached required fields, not an LLM reduction. For chat we can accept smaller model.
[03:48] Samir Patel: Yes, per-route and per-model policies are standard. You can tag routes as "safety-critical" and define fallback chains: for checkout route -> no model fallback, try cached then block; for chat route -> model fallback to smaller variant then cached.
[04:05] Priya Rao: Network security: if we go Dedicated or Private, we need VPC peering, SAML SSO, HSM/KMS for keys, and full audit logs. Can Redwood provide an on-prem control plane or do we need Private deployment?
[04:16] Julia Chen: We support Dedicated with customer VPC peering and KMS integration. For full on-prem or air-gapped control plane that's our Private offering. Both provide SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. We'll include architecture diagrams in the follow-up.
[04:30] Mark Lyle: How do you handle keys for model weights and logs? Are logs stored in Redwood-managed storage by default? We need to ensure PII never leaves our VPC.
[04:39] Samir Patel: For Dedicated we can arrange that logs and usage data are stored in your cloud project or in an encrypted Redwood account with customer-managed keys. For Private we can keep everything inside your network. We'll include the KMS/HSM integration notes in the security pack.
[04:54] Ethan Kim: We run a compliance review — SOC 2 Type II, ISO? Do you have those?
[04:59] Samir Patel: Yes, SOC 2 Type II available; ISO in progress. We'll send the attestation and the security pack (redwood.com/security.pdf as a placeholder link in the follow-up).
[05:10] Priya Rao: Back to failover: how do you avoid double-processing when a client retries and the service actually succeeded but response got lost? We need idempotency or exactly-once for some endpoints.
[05:20] Julia Chen: For idempotency we recommend request-id + idempotency-key patterns on client side with our SDK; on server side we support idempotent handling for non-streaming ops and token-resume semantics for streaming. For exact once you can persist outputs to your datastore after confirmation and use transactional patterns.
[05:38] Mark Lyle: Can Redwood do canary deploys and automatic rollback if latency/regression is detected?
[05:44] Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood Console supports canary rollouts and auto-fallback policies. You can define evaluation metrics (p95 latency, token cost, quality regressions tied to eval sets) and automatic rollback thresholds.
[05:57] Ethan Kim: For our perf tests — we want a baseline run using our prompts under synthetic load and then a stress test to simulate region failure. Can Redwood run those?
[06:05] Julia Chen: We can run joint benchmarks. For Dedicated we can provision a test pool and run replay of your traces. We'll need a dataset, traffic profile, and network diagram. We'll include a perf test plan in the tech deep dive.
[06:18] Priya Rao: On pricing, our finance team needs committed capacity pricing with clear overage rules. Dedicated monthly commit + burst sounds reasonable.
[06:26] Samir Patel: We'll share a draft pricing doc — reserved capacity tiers with burst to hosted, and pre-negotiated overage rates. We'll surface cost per token and per-hour for reserved GPUs.
[06:36] Mark Lyle: Any customers doing multi-region active-active with you? Any post-mortems we can see?
[06:42] Samir Patel: We have a few references in retail and fintech. We'll anonymize and share high-level runbooks and an incident summary that shows typical failover timelines and mitigations.
[06:53] Ethan Kim: A couple of nitty-gritty things: client SDK backoff settings, health-check endpoints, and the format of the audit logs.
[07:01] Julia Chen: SDK sets sensible defaults but you can customize retry/backoff. Health-check is a lightweight /health that returns primed status and region load. Audit logs are JSON events with request-id, user, model, tokens, and redacted input if requested. We'll include sample logs.
[07:17] Priya Rao: Do you have any built-in throttling or per-tenant isolation to prevent noisy neighbors from impacting our latency?
[07:24] Samir Patel: Yes, per-tenant quotas, priority queues, and autoscale isolation. For Dedicated you get isolated GPU pools; for Hosted we do soft isolation and priority lanes.
[07:36] Mark Lyle: For worst-case incident scenarios, do you provide a playbook? E.g., if regional control plane is down, how do we roll to secondary region manually?
[07:44] Julia Chen: We provide runbooks and one-click failover controls in the Console, plus an API to trigger routing changes. For Dedicated customers we also supply a runbook repo and optional runbook onboarding workshops.
[07:58] Ethan Kim: Can we define per-route SLOs and get alerting hooks to our PagerDuty?
[08:03] Samir Patel: Yes. Per-route SLOs, thresholds, and alert integrations (PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Slack) are supported.
[08:11] Priya Rao: A little noise: I've seen examples where fallbacks returned stale cached answers and caused a bug in checkout. Can we set TTLs and cache invalidation policies?
[08:19] Julia Chen: Cache TTLs are configurable by route. We also support cache keys based on request hashing and allow manual invalidation via API.
[08:28] Mark Lyle: For the model fallback chain, how do we ensure the smaller model is compatible and won't hallucinate on structured outputs?
[08:35] Julia Chen: We recommend validation rules — for structured outputs we run schema validation and can attach rerankers or a verification function. If the fallback fails validation, we have options: promote to human review, return error, or attempt cached canonical response.
[08:51] Ethan Kim: This is helpful. What's the likely recommendation for us — Hosted, Dedicated, or Private?
[08:56] Samir Patel: Based on scale, latency targets, and data needs you described, Dedicated looks like the best fit: predictable capacity, VPC peering, KMS, and the ability to run active-active across two regions. Private if you need on-prem/air-gapped control plane.
[09:08] Priya Rao: Ok. Next concrete steps?
[09:11] Samir Patel: We'll: 1) send SOC2/security pack + sample architecture diagram; 2) draft Dedicated pricing and capacity estimate; 3) schedule the tech deep dive (Julia lead) to map perf tests and network diagram. Anything else?
[09:24] Ethan Kim: Please add an estimated timeline for provisioning Dedicated capacity — how long from signed PO to live?
[09:29] Samir Patel: Typically 4–6 weeks for initial Dedicated provisioning and onboarding; can be faster with standard configs. We'll put exact timelines in the proposal.
[09:39] Mark Lyle: Thanks — can you also include a sample canary policy and rollback triggers?
[09:43] Julia Chen: Yes, will include a sample canary policy and the Console screenshots.
[09:48] Samir Patel: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and propose times for the tech dive.
[09:55] Ethan Kim: Appreciate it.
---
